title: Week 4: Post-Growth Economics and Plural Economies
text:
Week 4 Lecture · 90 min



What is the economy for? This session challenges the growth imperative at the heart of mainstream economics and introduces pluralist alternatives — ecological economics, degrowth, post-growth, and care economics — that make different assumptions about what an economy should prioritise and how it should be organised.

title: Week 4: Post-Growth Economics and Plural Economies
text:
Session Overview



Format
Lecture


Duration
90 minutes


Preparation for participants
~45 minutes reading

title: Week 4: Post-Growth Economics and Plural Economies
text:
Learning Objectives

Critique the GDP growth paradigm from an ecological and social perspective.
Describe the main tenets of ecological economics, degrowth, and post-growth frameworks.
Compare neoclassical and heterodox economic frameworks on the question of sustainability.
Evaluate the political economy of transitioning away from growth dependency.

title: Week 4: Post-Growth Economics and Plural Economies
text:
Session Outline

1. The problem with GDP (15 min)

What GDP measures and what it misses; historical context (Kuznets’ original warning); Easterlin paradox; GDP vs. well-being indicators (HDI, Genuine Progress Indicator, Happy Planet Index).

2. Ecological economics (20 min)

The economy as a subsystem of the biosphere; throughput (matter-energy flows); limits to growth revisited; steady-state economy; Herman Daly’s principles.

3. Degrowth and post-growth (25 min)

Degrowth vs. post-growth distinction; key claims (GDP growth drives ecological overshoot; redistribution over growth; sufficiency rather than efficiency); political feasibility and critiques; Global South perspectives — is degrowth a Northern luxury?

4. Care economy and feminist economics (15 min)

Unpaid care work; the iceberg economy; why sustainability transformations require recognising reproductive labour.

5. Discussion: Growth, development, and the Global South (15 min)

Should post-growth apply universally? What does “enough” mean across different contexts?

title: Week 4: Post-Growth Economics and Plural Economies
text:
Materials
Required reading

Hickel, J. (2020). Less Is More. Chapter 2: The birth of growth. (~30 pp.)
Raworth, K. (2017). Doughnut Economics. Chapter 7: Be agnostic about growth.
Norgaard, R.B. (1994). The case for methodological pluralism. Ecological Economics, 1(1). (Sections 1–2 only)

Optional

Kallis, G. (2018). Degrowth. Chapters 1–2.
Mies, M. & Shiva, V. (1993). Ecofeminism. Chapter 1.

title: Week 2: Planetary Boundaries and Sustainability Frameworks
text:
Week 2 Lecture + Workshop · 90 min



Building on the polycrisis framing from Week 1, this session goes deeper into the planetary boundaries science and introduces complementary frameworks — in particular Kate Raworth’s Doughnut model — for thinking about how social foundations and ecological ceilings interact.

title: Week 2: Planetary Boundaries and Sustainability Frameworks
text:
Session Overview



Format
Lecture + Workshop


Duration
90 minutes


Preparation for participants
~30 minutes reading

title: Week 2: Planetary Boundaries and Sustainability Frameworks
text:
Learning Objectives

Explain the scientific basis for at least five planetary boundaries, including key tipping point dynamics.
Describe the Doughnut model and explain how it relates social and ecological dimensions.
Apply a sustainability framework to evaluate a development policy choice.
Articulate tensions between economic development goals and planetary boundaries.

title: Week 2: Planetary Boundaries and Sustainability Frameworks
text:
Session Outline

1. Planetary boundaries: science and debate (30 min)

The latest boundary updates (Richardson et al. 2023); which boundaries are most transgressed; scientific uncertainties and ongoing debates; how boundaries relate to one another (Earth system interactions).

2. The Doughnut model (20 min)

Social foundation (12 dimensions from the SDGs) + ecological ceiling (based on planetary boundaries); the “safe and just space”; national and city-level Doughnut analyses.

3. Workshop: Applying the Doughnut (30 min)

Small groups apply the Doughnut model to a development scenario (infrastructure project, agricultural expansion, urban growth). Each group maps social benefits and ecological risks, then shares findings.

4. Debrief and discussion (10 min)

What trade-offs emerged? Whose perspective determines where to draw the line?

title: Week 2: Planetary Boundaries and Sustainability Frameworks
text:

title: CDE - Open Education Resources
text:
About this course
This course was developed in 2023 by a tri-national (Swiss, Kenyan, and Ethiopian) project team of nine members, representing:

University of Bern, Switzerland (Centre for Development and Environment)
Addis Ababa University, Ethiopia (Water and Land Resource Centre, and College of Education and Behavioral Studies)
University of Nairobi, Kenya (Department of Geography, Population and Environmental Studies, and the Centre for Training and Integrated Research on ASAL Development)

The team iteratively built and revised the course’s four sessions through collaborative working groups. The course was first piloted online with higher education faculty in Kenya in 2024, and on-site in Ethiopia in 2025. Following revision based on both pilots, it is now available for wider adoption.

Course objective
The course is designed to empower higher education lecturers in Ethiopia and Kenya with the knowledge, tools, and strategies to effectively integrate sustainable development (SD) and SD concepts and theories into their teaching. It provides an in-depth understanding of key SD concepts and theories, guides participants in establishing thematic connections between sustainable development and their own field, and highlights the importance of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) for sustainable futures.


Target group
The course is aimed at higher education teaching staff from all disciplines. Decision-makers and academic programme directors may also find it valuable to attend.


How you can use this course
There are several ways to engage with this material, depending on your needs:

Work through the course independently, at your own pace: All four sessions, materials, and exercises are freely available for self-paced learning — use them as they are, or draw on individual sections and materials for your own purposes.
Adapt and deliver the course at your own institution: The sessions, examples, and exercises can be localized to your own context — the illustrative cases used throughout (from Switzerland, Ethiopia, and Kenya) are meant as models, not fixed content, and are designed to be substituted with examples relevant to your own setting.
Co-design a course with us: If you are interested in developing a tailored version of this course together with the original project team, we welcome the opportunity to collaborate — please get in touch to discuss what this could look like [contact details to be confirmed].

title: CDE - Open Education Resources
text:
Course Sessions

The course consists of four sessions, each building on the previous one through a cumulative, individual project — the ESD Action Plan. Across the four sessions, participants develop their own ESD Action Plan: a concrete, ready-to-use lesson or session that integrates sustainable development into their own teaching, grounded in their own discipline and institutional context.







Foundations

Session 01: Introduction to Sustainable Development
Participants learn to define sustainable development and its core principles, identify key challenges that sustainability seeks to address.



View session







Foundations

Session 02: Interlinkages of Sustainability Dimensions and Role of Science & Education
Participants examine the links between social, economic, and environmental dimensions of sustainable development.



View session







Foundations

Session 03: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
Participants gain an understanding of the principles and importance of ESD as well as of the concept of constructive alignment in designing effective courses.



View session







Presentations

Session 04: Presentation of Action Plans
Participants present the action plan they have developed on how to integrate (E)SD into their own teaching. .



View session







Reflexions

Session 05: Reflection session
Participants provide feedback on course content, structure, etc.



View session

title: Adapt & Reuse
text:
Adapting This Course

This course is designed to be adopted and adapted by Higher Education Institutions worldwide. Everything here — sessions, slides, frameworks, assessment designs — is published under CC BY 4.0. You are free to take what you need, leave what you don’t, and build something better. This page explains how.




1. Use individual sessions
You do not need to run the whole course. Any session can stand alone as a guest lecture, workshop module, or seminar input. Each session page is self-contained with learning objectives, materials, tasks, and a localisation note.
How: Download the session QMD file from GitHub, or copy the content into your own course design.


2. Swap in local case studies
Every session includes a localisation note — a yellow panel at the bottom of the page — that guides you on how to replace our default examples (often European or generic global) with cases from your own regional context.
How: Follow the localisation note. If you develop a strong local example, please share it via a GitHub pull request so other institutions can benefit.


3. Translate
All materials are licensed for translation. A German version is in preparation at CDE. If you translate materials into another language, please notify the course team so we can link to your version from the repository.
How: Fork the GitHub repository, edit the QMD files, and publish your translated version.


4. Remix and extend
Add sessions, change the sequence, integrate your own assessments, or embed this course within a larger programme. The Quarto format makes structural edits straightforward.
How: Fork the repository. The _quarto.yml navigation and sessions/index.qmd listing control the structure. _variables.yml lets you update course metadata in one place.


5. Run a co-taught version
This course was designed for co-teaching across institutions. The case presentations (Weeks 9–10) and the field session (Week 11) are especially powerful when run jointly between partner institutions via video link.
How: Contact the CDE coordination team at cde@unibe.ch to discuss scheduling a joint cohort with another partner institution.


6. Contribute back
The course improves when institutions share what they changed and why. Contributions welcome: new case studies, updated readings, improved localisation notes, translations, additional sessions.
How: Open an issue or pull request on the GitHub repository. All contributors are acknowledged in the course team page.

title: Adapt & Reuse
text:
Technical Setup
The course is built with Quarto — an open-source scientific publishing system. You need Quarto installed to render the site locally.
Quick start:
# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/CDEteaching/[REPO-NAME].git
cd [REPO-NAME]

# 2. Install Quarto (see https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/)

# 3. Preview locally
quarto preview

# 4. Render to _site/ folder
quarto render
Deployment to GitHub Pages is automated via the included GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml). Push to main and the site rebuilds automatically.
Editing in RStudio: Open the project folder in RStudio — it will detect the Quarto project automatically. Use the Render button to preview individual pages.

title: Resources
text:
Reflection Journal Guidelines
The reflection journal is a weekly 300–400 word entry responding to a prompt from each session. Entries are submitted via the course platform within one week of each session.
Grading: Journals are graded holistically at the end of the course on depth of engagement (40%), use of course concepts (40%), and intellectual honesty — including expressing genuine uncertainty (20%). There is no penalty for “wrong” answers; the journal rewards careful thinking.

title: Session 1: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Week 1 Lecture · 90 min Plenary



The opening session introduces students to the concept of the polycrisis — the simultaneous intensification of interconnected crises (climate, biodiversity, inequality, geopolitical instability) — and makes the case for why incremental reform is insufficient. By the end, students should understand why transformation is both necessary and contested.

title: Session 1: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, students will be able to:

Participants learn to define sustainable development and its core principles, identify key challenges that sustainability seeks to address.
Participants discuss the relevance of sustainable development in their country contexts.

title: Session 1: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Session Outline


1. Opening provocation (15 min)

What does “sustainable development” mean to you? Brief pair discussion and plenary report-back.

2. The polycrisis concept (20 min)

Origins of the term (Adam Tooze); how compounding crises interact; why conventional risk analysis breaks down.

3. Planetary boundaries (25 min)

The nine planetary boundaries framework (Rockström et al., Steffen et al.); current status of each boundary; hotspots of transgression; equity dimensions (who transgresses, who suffers).

4. From crisis to transformation (20 min)

Incremental vs. structural change; the case for sustainability transformations; why transformation is contested (winners and losers, path dependencies, power).

5. Closing reflection (10 min)

One-minute paper: “What surprised you? What questions remain?”

text:

During the session
Add in-class activities, discussion questions, or workshop instructions here.









After the session

title: Session 1: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Recommendation for facilitation

The opening pair discussion (step 1) often surfaces wide variation in prior knowledge. Use this to frame the course as exploratory, not a transmission of fixed truths.
In the planetary boundaries segment, avoid the temptation to present the framework as settled science — acknowledge ongoing debates about thresholds, especially for novel entities and functional diversity.
Students from climate-vulnerable regions often have strong experiential knowledge of multiple crises. Create space for this — it will be valuable throughout the course.

title: Week 3: Socio-Technical Transitions and Transformation Theory
text:
Week 3 Lecture + Workshop · 90 min



This session closes the foundations block by introducing theories of change for sustainability transformations. Students encounter the Multi-Level Perspective (MLP) on socio-technical transitions, transition management, and Meadows’ leverage points — building a toolkit for the case-study work in later weeks.

title: Week 3: Socio-Technical Transitions and Transformation Theory
text:
Session Overview



Format
Lecture + Workshop


Duration
90 minutes


Preparation for participants
~30 minutes reading

title: Week 3: Socio-Technical Transitions and Transformation Theory
text:
Learning Objectives

Describe the Multi-Level Perspective (landscape, regime, niche) and apply it to a transition example.
Explain what leverage points are and identify at least three high-leverage intervention types.
Distinguish between technological, institutional, and cultural dimensions of sustainability transitions.
Assess the strengths and blind spots of transition frameworks (agency, power, justice).

title: Week 3: Socio-Technical Transitions and Transformation Theory
text:
Session Outline

1. The Multi-Level Perspective (25 min)

Landscape pressures, incumbent regime, niche innovations; transition pathways (substitution, transformation, de-alignment/re-alignment); example: energy systems in Kenya and Germany compared.

2. Transition management and governance (20 min)

Transition arenas; front-runner coalitions; backcasting; limits and critiques (who is at the table?).

3. Leverage points (20 min)

Meadows’ 12 leverage points; which interventions change a system most deeply (paradigms, goals, rules vs. parameters and feedback); application to climate and food systems.

4. Workshop: Where is the leverage? (20 min)

Groups map a transition they know (energy, food, mobility, land use) using the MLP and identify leverage points. Brief plenary sharing.

5. Synthesis and critical reflection (5 min)

What do these frameworks miss? (Power, colonialism, justice.)
